title: The 5 Big Ideas of English Language
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that English writing instruction can be organized around five big ideas rather than shifting fashions in grammar, exposure or text types. He briefly surveys decades of approaches and concludes they all worked in some measure because brains are meaning-making machines, but that none is simple. His five ideas cover verbs over nouns, imagery, sound at sentence level, conflict and contrast, and sentences that make sense. He then takes on The Writing Revolution, suggesting its sentence-level drills are being misapplied as an English curriculum when the book intends a whole-school approach built around content and, crucially, planning and revising. Finally he claims the reported gains owe more to a culture of hard work and changed student beliefs than to the writing method, citing his own school's experience.
points: Replace a sprawl of rules and criteria with five big ideas that can be the focus of every writing lesson, whatever the task.
Teach the five ideas as success criteria in creative writing as well as in analysis of texts.
Sentence-level drills without composing are like practising scales without ever playing music.
The Writing Revolution is better read as a whole-school approach to content than as an English writing curriculum, and schools often skip its planning and revising principle.
School culture and effort, rather than technique alone, may explain much of the improvement attributed to writing programmes.
quotes: Well, I’d like to suggest that, though they are 180% degrees apart in places, these approaches all worked. Everything works, because brains are learning machines, makers of meaning.

What if, instead of this, we can simply focus on the 5 Big Ideas of English language and writing. What if, no matter what the writing task, no matter what the context, we just have to focus on these 5 things?
But, to stretch the analogies, it is like learning the scales without every composing, or playing pieces of music. It is endless drills, with games played only once a month.

I think the issue with the way I have seen this applied is that schools have by and large ignored point 6, and tend not to teach essay writing in a meaningful way from year 7. And perhaps they have lost sight of 3 and 4 – the sentences themselves are not primarily models of good writing, they are intended as ways for students to better express their understanding of curriculum knowledge, or facts.
And this seems to me to be the underlying cause of success, even more than the quality of writing. Students had effectively been trained to work hard.

This had nothing to do with the quality of what they had been taught, and everything to do with the culture of the school. When we transformed the progress of students at Kingsdown school, introducing a culture of hard work was our first priority, way, way ahead of improving teaching.
It doesn’t mean they wouldn’t have improved much more with different methods. My money is on the 5 big ideas, and students reading and writing real texts.
